column5: Strong and broad-based economic growth in Ethiopia, averaging around 10.6 percent a year since 2005, has brought reductions in poverty and improvements in wellbeing. The percentage of Ethiopians living below the national poverty line (US$0.6 per day) declined from 39 percent in 2004/05 to less than 30 percent in 2010/11. Strong economic growth has also been associated with a notable increase in life expectancy and progress towards the attainment of the Millennium Development Goals (MDG), particularly in gender parity in primary education, child mortality, HIV/AIDS, and malaria. Notwithstanding these positive developments important challenges remain and need to be addressed to ensure sustainable poverty reductions and continuous economic growth. The growth rate of the real GDP per capita declined from 8.8 in 2005/06 to 7.9 in 2009/10. The absolute number of poor is almost the same as 15 years ago, 25 million, and a significant portion of the population remains just above the poverty line and is vulnerable to shocks. The number of nutrition-poor people has increased from 27 to 28.4 million between 2004/05 and 2010/11, and dependence on emergency relief remains persistently high, 9.6 million people in 2011. Furthermore, chronic under-nutrition, total fertility and maternal mortality remain at alarming rates. Overall, the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Index estimates the multidimensional poverty rate in Ethiopia to be 90 percent, the second highest after Niger of 104 developing countries covered. To succeed in meeting the GTP goals of reducing poverty, Ethiopia will need to sustain growth by transforming subsistence agriculture into a modern and more productive agriculture and changing the structure of the economy. Agriculture remains the cornerstone of growth. It accounts for almost 48 percent of GDP and 85 percent of export earnings, and it is the main income earner, livelihood and way-of-living for 85 percent of Ethiopians living in rural areas. A comprehensive approach to agricultural growth is needed, lowering population pressure on land as well as increasing efforts to improve women?s access to farm inputs, extension advice and credit. Efforts to diversify livelihoods and employment opportunities, supporting the expansion and development of micro and small enterprises, should complement agricultural growth to ensure faster and sustained development.Enabling the country to address these challenges requires building capacity of the public sector. A series of modernization efforts across the public service have contributed to more effective decision-making bodies and improved Government capacity to deliver results. However, continued efforts will be needed to build the capacity of the public service, both its institutions and human resources. The GTP fully recognizes human resource development and capacity building as the key strategic activities needed to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of public sector service delivery.Building analytical and statistical capacity and improving the evidence base for policy formulation, as proposed in this PKS, is an important part of this agenda. The CPS highlights the need for the Bank to find ways to engage more effectively with the GoE in policy dialogue on poverty and gender issues through increasing the relevance of the Bank?s economic and sector work and offering the GoE a menu of instruments available from across the World Bank Group. In this context, bridging the data and knowledge gap for evidence-based dialogue are key elements for success. The remainder of this note is structured as follows. Section II provides the context. Section III summarizes the objectives and links with GoE and Bank strategies. Section IV explains the PKS design. Section V presents the results framework. Section VI covers budget issues and highlights inter-sectoral collaboration. Section VII explains the quality control arrangements. Section VIII covers the counterpart and Section IX identifies risks.

column5: The proposed project under the TFESSD Trust Fund will pilot livestock insurance product development in collaboration with two World Bank projects in Ethiopia, in order to motivate farmers to invest in higher value livestock that will provide significantly highereconomic gains. Livestock contributes to a significant proportion of the income of small farmers in many developing countries. Additionally, it also contributes directly to the family's nutritional requirements and helps families cope during periods of crop failure.  However, very few countries have successful insurance programs that compensate farmers for the death of livestock, especially in risk-prone environments. This is the case in Ethiopia, a country that has one of the highest livestock to persons  ratios in  Africa. The proposed project under the TFESSD Trust Fund will pilot livestock insurance product development in collaboration with two World Bank projects in Ethiopia, in order to motivate farmers to invest in higher value livestock that will provide significantly higher economic gains.  This is expected to specifically benefit women who within households mostly take care of such  high-value animals and provide nutritional benefits to the whole family. The pastoral lowlands in Ethiopia encompass almost seven million people and over 11 million animals. Livestock production provides around half of pastoral incomes. The ongoing Pastoral Community Development Project II (PCDP II) supports the establishment and strengthening of Rural Savings and Credit Cooperatives (RUSACCOs) in selected pastoral communities, so that these RUSACCOs can provide financial services to the communities and help improve their livelihoods. The ongoing Food Security Project (FSP) is also involved in supporting RUSACCOs and livestock activities as part of its asset generation program. In the 1980s the World Bank had supported a livestock project in Ethiopia with a successful credit and insurance component based on  private sector participation. However, due to the profound political changes the project had to be abandoned.  The task team has had discussions with the Ethiopian experts involved at that time and they have agreed to work with the proposed pilot to re-introduce such insurance for higher-value animals. A local insurance company has been contacted by the one Ethiopian expert and has indicated an interest to be involved in the pilot. Indemnity insurance products for high value livestock have existed for a long time in the developed world and in parts of the developing world, particularly Asian countries such as India and Vietnam.  However, similar products offered at a significant scale  have not been reported from countries in Africa. Ongoing efforts in Kenya, Malawi and other African countries are related to the introduction of weather index-based crop insurance and possibly a pilot related to livestock (also index-based). These are potentially valuable tools to manage disaster risks related to extreme weather events but they are not suitable for risk management for smallholder farmers working with a small number of higher-value livestock. The proposed pilot thus fills a void and could potentially lead to scale-up and replication in other countries.

column311: Through a combination of results-based financing and TA, the proposed project will provide critical reform supporting investments and capacity building to the three public sector institutions - the central bank, NBE and two state owned banks, CBE and DBE - and improve the enabling environment for financial sector development. Project funds will be used to support the recapitalization of CBE and DBE and will support capacity building of the three public sector financial institutions.  The project has four components. Component 1 focuses on strengthening NBE?s supervisory mandate while the emphasis of Components 2 and 3 focus on targeted institutional reforms of the state-owned banks. Component 4 focuses on implementation support. Component 1: Strengthening the banking sector supervisory and regulatory framework and the institutional capacity of National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE): Support to NBE will include modernizing the banking regulation and supervision framework covering micro and macroprudential pillars, improving crisis preparedness, and strengthening capacity for financial market development. Component 2: Reform, restructuring and recapitalization of the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE): This component will support the reform and financial strengthening of CBE in line with the vision of a modernized CBE with a sound balance sheet, robust risk management and strengthened governance processes.   This will be sequenced to address firstly the reform of governance, secondly, the restructuring of the balance sheet to remove non-performing assets and reduce risk exposures.  Thirdly, to recapitalize the CBE to restore it to a positive capital position. No project funds will be used to support a line of credit or other financial intermediation activities. Component 3: Reform, recapitalization, and institutional strengthening of the Development Bank of Ethiopia (DBE): This component will support the transformation and institutional strengthening of DBE in line with the vision of a catalytic and well-governed DFI with a sound balance sheet, strong risk management and governance systems.  Additionally, the project will support the increase in capital of DBE to support its transformation and stability. No project funds will be used to support a line of credit or other financial intermediation activities. column5: The Government of Ethiopia is in the process of ratifying a new Social Protection Policy that lays out a vision for social protection in Ethiopia. Overall, this commits the Government to move beyond the partial, and fragmented, provision of social protection to establish a social protection system. Of critical importance is the commitment to extend the coverage of national safety net programs beyond the current focus on rural areas through the PSNP to include urban areas. Also, the Policy recognizes that not all households will graduate from the PSNP in rural areas, thus requiring a long-term safety net for the poorest in the country, particularly those who are labor poor and particularly vulnerable, such as older persons, orphans, among others. However, there is a risk that the Policy may remain unimplemented unless it is put into operation through the development of a Social Protection Strategy. This Strategy will translate the aspirations documented in the Policy into a concrete road map that will guide the design and implementation of social protection programs supported by Government and development partners. At the same time, there is need to capitalize on the Government?s interest in exploring the possible application of a safety net response to vulnerability in urban areas. This activity aims to provide a sound basis for further discussions on the national application of safety nets.  The Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs (MOLSA) has requested support from the World Bank to support the development of a Social Protection Strategy that will put the Social Protection Policy into operation. The aim of the Strategy is to move beyond the general commitments to establishing a social protection system that are articulated in the Policy to identify and sequence the introduction of priority social protection programs. The Strategy would also explore how to harmonize ? and scale-up ? existing initiatives that fit within these priorities. The process by which this Strategy is developed will be important to securing its success. There is a strong tradition of donor coordination in Ethiopia both within the social protection sector and beyond. The Social Protection Policy was the product of strong Government-donor collaboration. This way of working will be extended to the formulation of this Strategy to cement Government leadership in this sector and to strengthen and formalize the mechanisms for donor coordination. More importantly, investing in these processes is expected to result in greater support for the Strategy and thus improve the probably of its success, and eventual donor funding, as needed, for the proposed programs. The Government has also requested the World Bank to support the development of an urban safety net to complement the Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), which currently services chronically food insecure rural areas. The proposed work on the strategy will therefore also be used to work with Government to detail a more strategic response to vulnerability in urban areas drawing on both existing urban-based responses and the lessons learned from the rural safety net. This work includes an analysis to update and deepen the assessment of existing urban-based safety net responses, which in turn will form the basis for more detailed recommendations on the key design features of a national urban safety net program. This work will be led by the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs in coordination with the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development (MOFED), the National Social Protection Platform and relevant urban institutions to ensure broad-based support for the resulting concept note.

column3: Building Opportunities for Optimized Trade and Investment for Growth in East Africa
column5: To reduce trade costs, increase investment flows and finance for exports in participating countries in East Africa. Ethiopia (Phase I), Kenya and South Sudan, Djibouti, Somalia (Phase II) and Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda (Phase III)
column311: HoAI has been an important entry point to promote AfCFTA implementation in East Africa. As such, it has developed three roadmaps : (i) the Regional Trade Facilitation Roadmap 2022-2025; (ii) the Regional Private Sector Engagement Roadmap 2024-2028; and (iii) the Roadmap for Accelerating Development in the Borderlands of the Horn of Africa 2024-2028 . Moreover, the operation builds on several analytical pieces including core country diagnostics by the WBG and others.  These can be found in Annex 5. This project will have the following components :Component 1: Trade and Investment measures to enable private capital. Sub-component 1.1: More and better tradeImplementing trade commitments. BOOST will implement activities that encourage trade but utilize the implementation of existing trade commitments particularly AfCFTA , and other global (World Trade Organization -WTO), regional (HoAI, EAC, IGAD) initiatives that aim to promote trade. The key focus area here is to a) support country-level AfCFTA /EAC/HoAI implementation strategies, roadmaps and action plans (including enabling regulations to foster digital trade); and b) develop the capacity required within trade ministries and other technical agencies for trade related areas including trade negotiations and remedies, agricultural trade, and structured commodities trading. Improving trade efficiency: Support will be provided to implement an automated, coordinated and risk-based approach to trade in goods. This would include technical assistance and key investments to (i) facilitate trade and reduce non-tariff barriers including streamlining processes, implementation of risk management and coordinated border management, particularly for women and SMEs in border areas and inputs needed to support climate adaptation and mitigation efforts ; (ii) improve trade agency automation and payments within agencies, and interconnectivity between agencies within and across countries, with a focus on Customs, agricultural trade, standards, and national single windows; and (iii) digital trade including building an enabling environment for e-commerce through streamlined regulatory requirements, adopting verification systems for cross-border transactions, and leveraging digital payments implemented under component 1.2. An emergency preparedness plan, training and awareness raising for moving key goods in crisis will also be supported.Sub-component 1.2: More and better investmentsImplementing investment commitments. BOOST will support the implementation of global (WTO), continental (AfCFTA), and bilateral (e.g. Kenya-US), negotiations and commitments, which is especially critical given trade trends within the current political economy. The key focus area is to (i) support countries to implement AfCFTA?s Investment Protocol and the WTO Investment Facilitation Agreement; and (ii) develop the capacity required within investment departments and other technical agencies including on investment negotiations, promotion and development. The project will also pay special attention to regulations and restrictions that could prevent local and foreign investors from investing in projects that could support climate adaptation and mitigation efforts (e.g. renewable energy, waste management, eco-tourism, sustainable land use, etc.).Component 2: More and better financing for exportsSub-component 2.1: Scaling up trade finance for high potential MSME exporters This subcomponent will offer a set of activities to empower exporter SMEs with inclusive access to trade finance to better take advantage of agreements such as AfCFTA. This includes value chain financing solutions through AFREXIM or similar institutions to facilitate the growth and expansion of MSME exporters. This will also encompass funding resources to expand the availability of direct credit and the development of broader targeted financing products and services, such as measures to accelerate payments processing for trade receivables across suppliers. To the extent possible, activities under this subcomponent will leverage existing platforms and institutions and foster the use of digital approaches.  Additionally, capacity-building programs will be provided to eligible Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs) and MSMEs to build their knowledge of trade finance products and financing solutions. This is aimed to promote efficiency and build trust in cross-border trade transactions. Sub-component 2.2: De-risking and trade insuranceThis subcomponent will provide instruments to facilitate access to credit in export value chains, especially for SMEs and firms operating in FCVs. Through risk-sharing instruments such as guarantees or trade credit insurance, this component will facilitate access to credit from financial institutions on better terms (de-risking the riskier segments such as SMEs and firms in FCVs so that less collateral is required from lenders). Trade insurance through regional agencies like MANSA will also be deployed to mitigate risks for exporters. The subcomponent will prioritize a value-chain oriented approach to ensure strategic support of high-potential export value chains.Sub-component 2.3: Improving cross-border digital paymentsThis subcomponent aims to facilitate the adoption of technologies for efficient cross border payments, both inter and intra-regionally. This is expected to: i) Reduce transaction costs and overhead fees in trade transactions; ii) Facilitate seamless information sharing between exporters and financial institutions; iii) Improve market access for SME exporters venturing into new territories; and iv) Unleash opportunities for exporters to expand and diversify their products and services to new markets .Component 3: Regional coordination and Project ManagementSub-component 3.1: Regional coordinationThis component will support regional coordination for both components 1 and 2. In component 1, the primary focus will be on AfCFTA and its Secretariat, leveraging existing regional coordination mechanisms of the RECs (i.e. AfCFTA, EAC, IGAD and others) and platforms (i.e. HOAI  and others) with focused activities to bring together participating countries. Under component 2, regional coordination will be with regional financial institutions. Activities in both components on regional coordination will include organizing meetings and workshops for participating countries to develop and monitor joint action plans and coordinate with development partners and projects. Critically, this component will also support active engagement mechanisms with the private sector, particularly those outlined through the private sector engagement roadmap. The Project Implementation Units (PIUs) of participating countries will fund these activities.Sub-component 3.2: Project ManagementThis component aims to finance the operations, staffing, and activities of Project Implementation Units (PIUs) within the finance or trade ministries of participating countries, enhancing their capacity for daily management and implementation of the project alongside regional coordination. It will support the hiring of specialist positions and utilize existing staff for effective project execution including for fiduciary activities. Additionally, the component is dedicated to implementing environmental and social safeguards, developing and maintaining a grievance redress mechanism (GRM) for addressing complaints, including gender-based violence (GBV) issues, through potentially a shared platform. It will ensure a regional presence of PIUs in focus areas, including safeguards, and finance monitoring and evaluation (M&E) efforts, such as the Geo-Enabling Initiative for Monitoring and Supervision (GEMS), gender analysis, and sector-based surveys for assessing project progress. Furthermore, it will cover communications and stakeholder coordination activities, managed by the PIUs, with all activities and data collection being gender disaggregated.

column2: Ethiopia Education Transformation Operation for Learning
column3: Ethiopia Education Transformation Operation for Learning
column311: The Ethiopia Education Transformation Operation for Learning (ETOL) aims to increase equitable access and improve learning outcomes in pre-primary and primary education. To achieve this, the operation focuses on two interconnected results areas (RAs). The first RA focuses on transforming teaching and learning by enhancing teacher preparation and continuous professional development, providing high-quality learning materials, and strengthening school leadership. The second RA focuses on transforming schools into effective learning centers through expanded and improved school infrastructure, inclusive education support, and a targeted school grants system linked to School Improvement Plans (SIPs). Additionally, ETOL seeks to strengthen the education system and builds institutional capacity, with particular emphasis on the rollout of education technology (EdTech) solutions to enhance both system management and classroom practices. The operation combines national-level reform and capacity building with regionally tailored resource allocation, ensuring that all interventions contribute to improved learning outcomes and equitable access across Ethiopia.An Additional Financing (AF) is proposed to expand the scope of the parent operation to reach refugee preprimary and primary schools outside of the national education system and host community schools. This will be achieved through: (a) the provision of a minimum service support package to refugee and host community schools to strengthen pathways for equitable access, enhance teacher quality and availability, improve school leadership, and ensure adequate provision of teaching and learning materials so that schools progressively meet national standards; (b) the integration of primary refugee schools, which often include preprimary education, into the national education system; and (c) scaling up existing activities under the parent operation to support to refugee and host community schools.

column3: Mainstreaming Citizens Engagement in Bank Operations in Ethiopia
column5: The proposed activity is an economic and sector work (ESW) to take stock of experiences from existing fragmented citizens? engagement interventions in different projects in Ethiopia and consolidate lessons to inform and guide mainstreaming of CE in current, pipeline and future projects, and knowledge operations. the task will also involved analysis of data from the key CE interventions like the Ethiopia Social Accountability Program 2 (ESAP2) and the Financial Transparency and Accountability (FTA) component which have had baseline surveys and endline surveys are also envisaged before closure. Proposing this task is based on premise that establishing a systematic mechanism for engaging citizens in the Ethiopian context can foster better reflection of citizens needs in project interventions, assure beneficiary participation and ownership of Bank supported operations, contribute to building of an effective system for CE and lead to improved results on the ground. The proposed work would take forward recommendations from the Bank wide corporate ?Strategic Framework for Mainstreaming Citizens Engagement in World Bank Group Operations, December 2014?, and through a review of existing and pipeline projects, consultations with government, private sector and civil society organizations, and propose recommendations on how to feasibly customize the framework to the Ethiopian context and generate tailored recommendations for sustainable mainstreaming of CE in Bank supported operations.The work will involve a two year economic and sector work program from FY16 to FY17 and extension to FY18 will be considered based on actual progress in FY17. The task will evolve from concept development, documentation of experiences, consultations on findings and elaboration of recommendations together with consultations among a wide range of stakeholders and agreements to apply the recommendations to pipeline operations and those that will undertake mid-term reviews after FY16 in the first and second years. In addition, there will be a dissemination and monitoring of findings in FY17 and FY18, and sustained creation of awareness about the recommendations among government and project teams alongside an evaluation of applicability of recommendations.	The proposed task would introduce a new knowledge program that seeks to span beyond specific projects/programs with a strong systematic, knowledge generation and learning approach. It would complement the existing knowledge programs by focusing on a combination of demand-side and supply driven citizens engagement activities in a pro-poor manner, and would seek to identify approaches, mechanisms, measurements and means of verifications for applying citizens engagement with specific focus on development, basic service delivery and inclusive participation by the citizenry, with a strong emphasis on the poor and vulnerable.The following deliverables are expected.FY16: 1. A Work Plan for Implementation of the Task.  The focus, specific content and methodology of the other two deliverables will be informed by this work plan; 2. A Methodological Guide for Mainstreaming Citizens Engagement in Bank Operations in Ethiopia: The deliverable will result from rapid desk reviews, consultations and focus group discussions.FY 17: 3. Lessons from Systematic Initiatives on Citizens Engagement in Bank Projects in Ethiopia: This deliverable will draw from experiences in implementing the Ethiopia Social Accountability Program phase 2 (ESAP2), the Financial Transparency and Accountability (FTA) program, and the Grievance Redress Mechanism under the PBS3. The deliverable will draw from the ongoing separate evaluations for each programs for which baselines have been completed and end line surveys are expected. It will provide an opportunity to make a case for value for money of the CE work providing evidence of what has worked, the impacts and bring to light the desired improvements in design and implementation.

A planned interconnection between the Ethiopian and Kenyan systems will enablethe development of the huge hydro power resources in Ethiopia at a considerable low cost due to reasons of economies of scaleThe proposed Gibe III HPP will be an 1870 MW hydropower project in the Omo-Gibe river basin in Ethiopia (the Project).For the construction of Gibe III, Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation (EEPCo), the state owned electricity utility, has enteredinto an Engineering, Procurement and Construction turnkey contract with Salini Costruttori S.p.A. (Italy) with the understandingthat the Electro-mechanical and Hydro-mechanical works will be undertaken by international competitive bidding.  The EPC contractis estimated at Euro 1.45 Billion. The project is currently expected to receive financing from the Government of Ethiopian (GOE),the European Investment Bank, AfDB and from the Government of Italy (loans to GOE) in addition to internal cash generation byEEPCo.  However, such financing is not expected to cover the entire project cost and an additional Euro 300 to 500 million willneed to be mobilized for the project.Such large amounts of financing cannot are unlikely to be raised in the public market.  The proposed assessment would allowcommercial, bilateral and multilateral lenders to assess the project's technical, financial and economic viability, and support themobilization of private commercial loans for Gibe III.  A secondary objective is also to enable Ethiopia to begin tapping theprivate lending institutions for infrastructure developments - this project would be the first to be supported by privatefinancing.  Given the large hydropower potential of Ethiopia, a financing strategy for large generating projects must include themobilization of private financing and private expertise in development, implementation and operations of such projects.The World Bank Group is proposing to support to GOE in mobilizing the necessary additional financing from the private/commercialloan markets thru the use of Bank Group guarantees against certain political risks. Given that the next generation plants in thepipeline are all large sized projects, mobilization of financing with Bank support is expected to have a signaling effect in theinternational bank markets. column311: The proposed project supports the implementation of the World Bank?s Country Partnership Framework for Ethiopia (CPF FY18 to FY22) to promote structural and economic transformation through an inclusive and market-based approach to contribute to economic recovery and job creation. It complements ongoing engagements of the World Bank Group in terms of addressing macro-fiscal constraints through the policy operations and through assessing the impact of the conflict, challenges in access to finance, trade logistics, and infrastructure (such as land and quality systems), investment climate, and by strengthening the financial sector.This project has four components:Component 1: Supporting inclusive and resilient growth (indicative allocation: $45 million)This component will address the need to recover and build a private sector that is more inclusive and resilient to promote equitable growth, particularly for marginalized population, and to support enterprises that are providing market solutions to rising climate change and sustainability challenges. This component will have two subcomponents: (a) Subcomponent 1.1. Growing SMEs that Employ Women and Youth. This subcomponent aims to support the growth of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) that have majority employment of women, youth, and/or marginalized populations. Given that unemployment was exacerbated during COVID, supporting SMEs that focus on hiring female or youth employees, and marginalized populations, would help to rebuild a more inclusive workforce. The project will leverage existing programs and intermediaries serving inclusive employment SMEs, to provide the enterprises with capacity building, technical assistance, financial credit readiness, and access to markets?including public and corporate procurement? to grow the demand for their products; and (b) Component 1.2. Leveraging Social Businesses and Green Enterprises for Inclusive Socio-Economic Growth. This subcomponent will support the growth of enterprises that incorporate social and/or environmental considerations into their business model for a more inclusive and sustainable growth. Social businesses and social enterprises tackle key development challenges?such as clean water access, access to energy, last-mile health services, youth employment, waste recycling, etc.?and often do so by employing from marginalized communities. The benefits are two-fold, addressing key development needs and providing inclusive employment. Moreover, social enterprises are often more resilient than traditional enterprises during crisis times?such as COVID?since they prioritize social impact over profit and are more likely to adapt and adjust their business model to maintain staff employment.Component 2: Supporting firm recovery (US$60 million)This component will support the domestic private sector to recover from COVID-19 and conflict impacts by broadening access to local and international markets that require firms to have competitive products and services that meet consumers? and international market requirements. Women and youth particularly face additional challenges to access markets, production facilities etc. due to lack of business network, access to finance, and so on. The component will finance three subcomponents:  Access to market for domestic SMEs; Speed up firm recovery through the integration of firms into Global Value Chains (GVCs); and Supporting innovation and technology adoption of firms. Component 3: Entrepreneurship development (US$ 30 million)This component will support the development of entrepreneurship as an enabler of creating a dynamic and innovative private sector. This will be achieved through: (i) the development of the legal and policy framework; (ii) access to finance; and (iii) skills development for firms.Component 4: Project Management and Monitoring and Evaluation (indicative allocation: US$15 million)The project will ensure integrated and effective planning, implementation, and coordination of the activities. It will actively support communication with key stakeholders including project interventions, implementation, and monitoring of fiduciary and safeguard policies and compliance, and progress monitoring and results evaluation. The project will establish a project coordination unit at federal level, which will be responsible for these activities. The project will ensure the development and implementation of a robust monitoring, evaluation, and learning system to track and evaluate project progress towards PDO, provide useful information for project management, and document and share project learnings. This component focuses on ensuring the implementation of the project in accordance with the financial, procurement, and environmental and social requirements and guidelines agreed. The project will ensure quality and timely reporting of financial, procurement, and Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) performance and audit reports. The project will finance project staff costs, consultants, equipment, capacity-building, and advisory services.

column5: The Government of Ethiopia has introduced MDG Specific Purpose Grant (SPG) in 2011 to support Regions in fulfilling MDGs. It is, therefore, necessary to take stock of the results of the performance of the financing modality. Accordingly, the Ethiopian Government formally requested the World Bank for a Just-in-time technical assistance (TA) to undertake the evaluation. Thus, the main purpose of the TA support is to provide an independent evaluation of the MDGs SPG in attaining the MDGs and the effectiveness of overall process of financing and implementation /modality. The TA will support the intention of the government to ensure that the MDGs fund arrangement provides the required assurance that the resources of the fund will be used for the intended purpose and scaling up. In this respect, the scope of this assignment is limited to evaluating the Government?s functions in the areas of MDGs grant arrangements/process, MDG grant result achievement, organizational and manpower capacities and supports for improving the performance of MDG grant system, along with, identifying challenges and lessons, proposing measures. The evaluation should be capable, in its analysis and presentation, of providing input to GoE for future decision to provide recommendations on future improvements for the designed financing modality.The task description for carrying out the evaluation focuses in the following four major areas:(i)	Conduct process evaluation on the context and design of MDG fund: The evaluation should respond to the following     questions: ? Was the MDG grant designed appropriately (given the context at the time of design) to enable the achievement of its development objectives? ? Was MDG grant channeled along with and through improved implementation of national systems? ? Should a restructuring of the MDG grant have been considered at any time during implementation? ? Were the grant implementation risks and mitigating measures correctly and adequately identified during design and were they addressed during implementation? ? The SPG was identified as the most appropriate instrument for channeling funds to Regions from MOFEC. Was this fully justified and were other alternatives considered and satisfactory reasons given for their rejection? ? What lessons have been learnt during the pilot in this regard? ? Has the MDG SPG managed to test and prove that a dedicated capital funding channel can significantly scale up capital funding in Regions and woredas to fulfill MDG targets? ? What are the remaining constraints and what measures need to be put in place to make it (or other alternatives) more sustainable with or without donor funding?(ii)	Conduct impact/outcome evaluation on effectiveness and sustainability of MDGs fund: The effectiveness and sustainability of MDG fund will be evaluated in terms of achieving its objective as a special capital investment /budget support in attaining the MDGs; and by defining attributions and links to Development objectives and outcomes. This will be evaluated taking into account the expected outcome indicators and lessons of experience of implementation /modality and the application of supports for the achievement and sustainability of results.(iii)	Conduct process evaluation on efficacy of sector/project implementation financed by MDG fund: The process evaluation should respond to the questions such as Has MDGs grant been used efficiently? What are the key factors that have had a significant impact on the implementation and performance of projects by MDG grant, and what lessons can be learned from these? etc.(iv) Evaluation of the institutional arrangement, implementation and performance of implementing agencies: The organizational structure, roles and capacities of involved institutions in leading, coordinating, overseeing, managing and administrating the investment process will be reviewed.

column2: Impact Evaluation of Electrification in Ethiopia
column3: Impact Evaluation of Electrification in Ethiopia
column5: The proposed work has two components: (i) Provide Technical support to EEPCO, for carrying out a rigorous socioeconomic impact evaluation of the universal access program, and (ii) Complementary impact evaluations focusing on the short-term policy-oriented issues.First, EEPCO is carrying out a rigorous impact evaluation to assess the actual benefits from its ongoing UEAP, an important and ambitious development agenda in Ethiopia. In recent years, significant progress has been made in rural electrification. However, there are still significant challenges ahead. 11,000 villages remain to be electrified. The mid-term national target is to increase power access to 75 percent by 2015. It is essential to verify the real benefits from the program and draw lessons learned to improve future program implementation, especially as the program extends to much remote areas. Close collaboration with timely technical inputs will be necessary for EEPCO to carry out the proposed evaluation, because it is a first ever full-fledged impact assessment for EEPCO. In addition, impact evaluation of an infrastructure project generally involves a number of technical and practical challenges, because random experiment is rarely allowed and the project life tends to be significantly long. The evaluation will examine social and economic benefits, focusing on: (i) household electricity use, (ii) productive use of power, (iii) educational benefits, (iv) health and fertility benefits, and (v) externalities, such as safety improvement due to street lighting. The proposed identification strategy is the difference-in-difference method based on a pipeline comparison with other evaluation methods combined such as matching and regression discontinuity if certain exogenous determinants of project placement exist. While further discussion and refinement will be required based on available data and project implementation schedule, the evaluation will be carried out using multiple techniques to ensure robustness of the possible estimation results.The Bank has been providing technical inputs to design this evaluation and will continue to support EEPCO to complete the evaluation successfully. This work is aimed at developing the client?s capability of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) and impact evaluation. The Bank will provide technical advice and guidance on sampling, questionnaire design, field survey framework and analytical work. Second, to complement the above assessment, the Bank will conduct its own impact evaluations focusing on particular policy issues. This primarily aims at inform sector policy dialog in the relatively short term. Ethiopia has embarked upon various innovative policy measures, such as energy efficiency programs and connection charge-financing. Among others, the power sector corrector installation program would likely be the first area of evaluation. Further discussion with EEPCO will be needed to determine other evaluation issues.In Ethiopia, the demand side management is increasingly recognized as an important measure to control the power demand, which has been increasing by more than 10 percent per annum. EEPCO is currently implementing a nonresidential energy efficiency program by installing 1,500 power factor correctors. This aims at increasing energy efficiency among large volume users and reducing peak power loads. On the residential side, EEPCO also implemented several CFL bulb distribution programs in recent years. In total more than 5 million bulbs were distributed, which seem to have saved about 13.3MW of peak energy demand.EEPCO is implementing a connection charge-financing program. In Ethiopia, households participating in the connection charge financing program pay 20 percent of the normal connection charge of $75 and the remaining 80 percent is collected will be collected through five-year installments. The effectiveness of these policy measures will be evaluated under the second component of this work.

The assessors reviewed the laws and regulations in place in Ethiopia and determined to what extent these are being applied in practice and how effective the Ethiopian authorities are at gathering financial intelligence and going after financial crime. While on paper most of the building blocks are in place, in practice capacity is relatively low, with only the financial intelligence unit really aware of and understanding how to implement its AML/CFT system. To improve the system the team recommended:1) Completion of the National Risk Assessment (NRA) process - To ensure that all AML/CFT stakeholders in Ethiopia have the same understanding of the risks they are seeking to address and working towards the same goals, and to ensure that the risk assessment process  consider Terrorism Financing risk given the potential TF risk.2) Broadening and reorientation of the reporting of suspicious transactions, analysis, and ML investigations, prosecutions and asset freezing and confiscation towards the most significant sources of illicit proceeds and identification of the most common ML methods/techniques. The National Risk Assessment should assist in identifying the most significant sources of criminal proceeds and the most common methods/techniques of ML within Ethiopia. This in turn should assist policy makers, reporting institutions and investigative agencies in turning their attention and resources to address these areas of higher risks so that ML provisions can be used to take the profit out of crime - be it corruption, tax fraud/evasion, human trafficking or smuggling contraband. In addition, it will be important that investigative and prosecutorial authorities start bringing cases before the Court as a means to ?test? the various provisions of the ML law, in particular the required level of proof of the predicate offence.  3) Provide further training and awareness raising for government officials and reporting entities - Given the fact that the AML/CFT system only started yielding results relatively recently and that many actors are not yet fully aware of their obligations or understand the ultimate objective, it will be important to ensure constant training in obligations of the reporting entities and government agencies, money laundering techniques, and ensuring awareness of the NRA findings (once completed) and how the government intends to address them. Given the likelihood that proceeds of crime are invested in real estate, it will be particularly important to ensure that real estate agents are made aware of their obligations under the AML/CFT legislation, and start inquiring into the source of funds.4) Expand financial services to the unbanked and those without access to financial services - Given the very high percentage of the population that is without access to financial services, and the estimated very high volumes of transactions taking place in cash, unrecorded and untraceable, it will be important to ensure that the efforts of the National Bank of Ethiopia and the (public) financial sector to expand access, by offering low value accounts through traditional banks and through micro-finance institutions5) Increase funding and staffing for the Financial Intelligence CenterThe above actions will assist Ethiopia in putting in place a robust defence against money laundering and terrorism financing, and ensure also that it can participate in the international financial system when it starts opening up it's domestic financial system to outside players.

While ratification of the policy is an important step forwards in terms of laying the foundation for a sustainable social protection system in Ethiopia, the SP Strategy identified the need for additional analysis to deepen understanding of the programming that is required to deliver on some of the focus areas. In this regard, the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MOLSA), which leads the social protection agenda in Ethiopia, has requested support from the World Bank for this additional analytical work. This proposed TA responds to this request and follows on from the previous technical assistance from the World Bank to MOLSA that played an important role in the formulation of both the Policy and Strategy. The proposed TA would focus on preparing a set of analytical products that would support the World Bank?s dialogue with the government to advance the social protection agenda and particularly the implementation of the SP strategy. The aim is to focus on forward looking areas that will be of increasingly strategic importance and have been relatively neglected to date. To this end, the proposed TA would focus on: (i) furthering the dialogue on social protection systems, with a particular aim of synthesis and broadening the lessons emerging from the system building work under the PSNP and the UPSNP; (ii) analyzing the existing contributory pension system and options for extending coverage to the informal sector; and, (iii) furthering analysis and understanding of labor markets and employment services as input to strengthening the delivery of labor programs in Ethiopia. In each of these areas, the team will draw on international expertise from across the World Bank; the labour market work will be carried-out together with the Poverty GP. Separate products will be prepared for each area, given their different nature and audiences.

column311: This hybrid operation?combining Program-for-Results (PforR) and Investment Project Financing (IPF)?supports the National Strategic Investment Framework for Sustainable Landscape Management (ESIF 2, 2024?2038) by advancing long-term landscape restoration. It aims to: (i) expand sustainable land management in degraded highland areas; (ii) sustain and expand certification, registration, and digitalization of rural land rights in Ethiopia?s highlands, including communal forests and grazing lands; and (iii) raise farm incomes and create jobs by strengthening agribusiness value-chain linkages. Primary beneficiaries are smallholder farmers in program watersheds. The program will increase smallholders? livelihood security and broaden income earning opportunities. Efforts will be made for the equitable inclusion of all beneficiaries in Community Watershed Users? Cooperative Societies (CWUCS) including vulnerable groups such as landless, youth, elderly, and female-headed households.The PforR component will finance watershed-level sustainable land and natural resource management, strengthen rural land administration, improve tenure security for private and communal lands (including selected forests and grazing areas), and catalyze private-sector participation to ensure sustainability. Under Result Area 1 (Participatory Watershed and Forest Management), Disbursement-Linked Indicators (DLIs) incentivize scaling up restoration and market linkages by: (1) registering Community Watershed Users? Cooperative Societies (CWUCS) with participatory, approved Watershed Management Plans; (2) expanding the area under sustainable landscape management; (3) establishing Participatory Forest Management with legally recognized cooperatives and approved Forest Management Plans; (4) treating acid soils; (5) integrating cooperatives into existing and new value chains within program catchments; and (6) verifying non forest emission reductions. Under Result Area 2 (Rural Land Administration), DLIs focus on expanding and digitizing secure tenure by: (1) issuing Second Level Land Holding Certificates (SLLCs) for individual parcels; (2) issuing SLLCs for communal forests and grazing lands; (3) operationalizing the National Rural Land Administration Information System in program woredas with digitized SLLCs; and (4) increasing connectivity of land administration offices and systems to national digital infrastructure. The IPF component?financed by IDA, SCALE, Nordic Development Fund (NDF), and ENABLE?will provide cross-cutting technical assistance and capacity building across both result areas and the broader government program (ESIF 2). It will support: (i) agribusiness development by linking landholders to agribusinesses; (ii) design and implementation of payment for ecosystem services (PES) schemes; (iii) access to carbon markets; and (iv) Operationalize pilots to promote voluntary land consolidation in Ethiopia?s highlands. These pilots involve baseline surveys, voluntary land exchange, and design, testing, and documentation of a computerized platform in real-world conditions. The likelihood and magnitude of risk for the voluntary exchange program pilot have been assessed. The voluntary land exchange will take place in 12 designated kebeles, involving small parcels of land and following a national legal proclamation.Targeted TA will also promote inclusive alternative livelihoods for women and youth through group-based training and livelihood grants; strengthen community capacity to scale ecosystem conservation and carbon sequestration via participatory forest and watershed management; advance land tenure and property rights awareness; and establish community-based performance monitoring. In addition, the operation will enhance MoA and Ethiopia Forest Development (EFD) operational capacity for CALM 2, including: (i) environmental and social risk management; (ii) procurement and financial management; and (iii) monitoring, reporting, and verification, including advanced remote sensing. IFC will complement implementation with integrated upstream and downstream support for agribusiness linkages, value-chain development, and access to finance, strengthening market access and supply chains through its portfolio, pipeline, and early-stage leads. IFC?s approach will promote business models that directly engage smallholder farmers and local communities, with close IFC? World Bank collaboration to ensure coordinated delivery.

Activities during this phase were: obtaining official support for the review process; undertaking a stakeholder analysis and selecting the participants who will carry out the review; drawing up a work program of the review process; and securing the technical and financial inputs. The selected participants formed a stakeholder group and, guided by a facilitation team, jointly assessed the country's poverty reduction and transport strategies in a series of three workshops. Meetings with other stakeholders were also organized, to feed in additional experiences and ideas. column311: The Power Sector Reform, Investment and Modernization in Ethiopia (PRIME) MPA program will support a medium-term transition of the electricity sector towards universal access, reliable supply, utility financial sustainability, increased private investments, and a climate resilient diversified generation mix. This transition will be underpinned by structural reforms that will encompass a gradual segregation of the competitive segments of the sector from the monopolistic segments to enable increased private participation under a competitive market regime. In parallel, the program will pursue operational reforms that will enhance utility financial sustainability through timely adjustment of tariffs, greater energy accountability, efficient investment planning, improved collections, reduced losses, and modernization of systems. This medium-term reform transition will be achieved through upfront adoption of a reform mandate by the Government, time-bound reform actions intertwined with investment support, and institutional capacity building to support the preparation and implementation of specific reform actions.Using a multi-phase approach, the PRIME program will support investments in expansion and strengthening of the electricity network to facilitate accelerated expansion of electricity access with improved reliability of supply. The program will also enable private sector investments in non-hydro renewable energy generation. The network strengthening investments under the PRIME will complement investments in last-mile electricity access under the ongoing ?Ethiopia Electrification Program (ELEAP)? and ?Access to Distributed Electricity and Lighting in Ethiopia (ADELE)? projects, as well as the Ethiopia phase of the upcoming ?Accelerating Sustainable & Clean Energy Access Transformation in AFE Region MPA? (ASCENT Ethiopia). Risk mitigation measures to enable private sector investments in non-hydro renewable energy generation will be co-supported by the ongoing Renewable Energy Guarantees Program (REGREP MPA). Together, these interventions will help Ethiopia achieve the triple goals of delivering universal electricity access, energizing faster economic growth, and establishing itself as a regional energy hub.The first phase of the PRIME program will improve the reliability and capacity of the electricity network in select towns and mitigate risks for private investments in non-hydro renewable energy through upstream preparation activities, while also establishing the medium-term sector reform trajectory. PRIME-1 project will improve the reliability and capacity of the electricity network in select towns and augment transmission with new lines and associated substations, while modernizing some aspects of the electricity systems. Building on the earlier success in geothermal resource establishment through drillings at Aluto Langano, this phase will establish geothermal resources for at least two new locations for subsequent private sector-led development under competitive selection modalities. Finally, this phase will oversee the adoption and initial implementation of the medium-term reform roadmap through a combination of capacity building and Performance-Based Conditions (PBCs) that will intertwine network investments with specific reform actions.The first component of the PRIME-1 project will improve the quality of supply in select towns across Ethiopia by rehabilitating the electricity distribution network. Power distribution networks in these towns are old and, in some extreme cases, have not been expanded or modified over the past decades. As a result, equipment failures and unplanned power outages are widely prevalent. Many of the wooden poles used to support the wires were installed over two decades ago and are now severely aged and unreliable. Further, these distribution network systems are now much overloaded. While on the one hand, it is difficult to meet the growing electricity demand imposed on these networks by new connections, on the other hand this causes higher technical losses and frequent unplanned interruptions. Distribution networks in these towns will be strengthened by reconfiguring and upgrading feeder conductors as well as transformers, and replacing poles and insulators as needed.This component will also provide technical assistance as well as institutional capacity building support to EEU specifically for structural and operational reforms. The key reforms at EEU that will be supported are: (i) Segregation of Public Service Obligations (PSO) from commercial business of EEU, (ii) Establishment of strategic business units (SBUs) along the regional EEUs, (iii) Tariff adjustments to reflect variations in inflation and currency exchange rate, and (iv) Least cost distribution expansion planning. The key areas identified for program level institutional capacity building are project management, contract administration, procurement, and safeguards (including environment, social, gender equality, health, and safety aspects).The second component will construct ten new substations and related transmission lines to ensure adequate transmission capacity for the above towns (and the surrounding areas) as well as four additional lines with substations to improve the overall grid reliability and carrying capacity. This component will also support the ?System Defense Project (SDP)? which involves modernization of the transmission grid by resolving the challenges of frequent system wide instability and outages due to miscoordination of primary, secondary, and tertiary frequency control systems and undamped oscillation issues.This component will also provide technical assistance as well as institutional capacity building support to EEP specifically for structural and operational reforms. In terms of reforms, support will be provided for (i) Accounting, functional, asset, and human resource separation across the Generation, Transmission, and System Operation functions of EEP, (ii) Tariff adjustments to reflect variations in inflation and currency exchange rate, and (iii) Least cost distribution expansion planning. The key areas identified for program level institutional capacity building are project management, contract administration, procurement, and safeguards (including environment, social, gender equality, health, and safety aspects).The third component will finance drilling for geothermal resource establishment at additional locations beyond the Aluto Langagno area (covered under GSDP) in preparation for private sector-led development of over 100MW geothermal power. Building on the successful drilling of wells at Aluto Langano, this sub-component will deploy existing drilling rigs owned by EEP (purchased under the GSDP) to further establish geothermal resources at two or more new locations that will be agreed during project preparation. These wells will supplement the wells currently being drilled at the Aluto Langano site under the GSDP and together establish a set of adequate geothermal resource for downstream development of a large geothermal power generation program.Component four of the PRIME-1 project will provide support to the regulator specifically for reform related technical assistance and capacity building.

column5: The proposed IDF grant aims at supporting the creation of a robust Accountancy profession from the existing non-professional grouping of accountants and auditing practitioners called Ethiopia Professional Accountancy and Auditors Association (EPAAA) within the country which will be well regulated. It will also strengthen the country#s quality of financial reporting through adoption and application of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) in private sector and public enterprises which contribute a significant portion of the country#s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). This will subsequently improve the system of accountability and good governance through an audit process that adopts the usage of International Standards on Auditing (ISA) in private and public sector companies. This will be achieved through the establishment of accounting and auditing regulatory body and a professional accountancy body to ensure that there is consistent and uniform application of the adopted standards that conform to international norms. Given the long standing absence of appropriate governance and management arrangements of the accountancy and auditing professions in Ethiopia, the grant also aims at establishing serious enforcement mechanisms of standards amongst its members through the regulatory bodies to be established. This will be done through (i) creation of new and modernized statutory framework for corporate financial reporting and auditing practices (ii) build capacity for professional accountants, auditors and regulators (iii) establishing regulatory and enforcement rules for accountancy and auditors and (iv) provide support to educational institutions to modernize accounting and auditing profession

column5: A 3-year programmatic and multi-sectoral development policy operation is proposed.  1. The introduction of development policy lending forms a core part of the Country Partnership Strategy.  The CPS states that ?as soon as macroeconomic framework allows, the budget support agenda will be resumed (most likely starting with sectoral development policy lending and over time moving towards multi-sectoral Development Policy Operations) to deepen policy dialogue and support GoE?s focus on achieving macroeconomic balance.?  2. Ethiopia?s macroeconomic framework is adequate for a development policy operation.  High economic growth is underpinned by macroeconomic stability.  Inflation has been brought under control in part because of tighter monetary policy.  Fiscal policy, driven by public capital accumulation, forms a core part of the economic strategy.  Although external borrowing is rising, the risk of external debt distress is manageable.  The external position is vulnerable shocks, but foreign reserves and the exchange rate are stable.  3. A DPO would lend support to Ethiopia?s nascent, but emerging, reform agenda.  Ethiopia is a country plenty of results, achieved in part on the back of reforms introduced in the earlier stages of the Meles Administration since 1991.  The reform momentum, however, has gradually petered out and no major reforms have been introduced in recent years.  International experience suggests that growth accelerations depend on continued institutional and structural reforms.  As constraints to growth become more binding under existing legal and regulatory frameworks, the incentives of the GoE are thus more likely to tilt in favor of continued reforms.  4. A number of recent and ongoing legal and administrative changes in agriculture, energy and trade logistics could form the basis for a Bank-supported Program.  Efforts to improve agricultural research, cooperatives, seed development and the input credit system could be one pillars of a multi-sectoral development policy operation.  Reforms in the energy sector, such as the increased openness to foreign investors and the administrative reform of the state-owned energy company EEPCO also merit Bank support. Finally, Ethiopia is taking steps to reduce the time and costs of trade through administrative reforms.  5. The analytical foundation for a DPO is strong.  Recent analytical work provides a stronger evidence base for understanding Ethiopia?s heterodox economic model, including its strengths and vulnerabilities.   Ethiopia?s impressive track record in inclusive growth, poverty reduction across a wide range of development indicators has also been well documented recently.  6. A Development Policy Operation in Ethiopia is a high-risk, high-return proposition.  GoE views on budget support operations are well known.  Success thus depends on genuinely strong government ownership of operational design.  Risk factors outside the control of the country team are also important to emphasize.  That said, a development policy operation brings important benefits in the form of strengthening the economic policy dialogue, supporting the GoE reform agenda to sustain development performance and can contribute to a continued successful portfolio performance.

column5: PPIAF funds are requested to implement the workshop on #Promoting Private Sector Participation in Roads and Highways# to be held in June 2002 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.  Some 60 participants from Ethiopia (35), Ghana (10), Uganda (7) and Tanzania (7) and donor representatives are expected to attend.  The three countries represent different levels of private sector development and participation in road projects.  All countries have previously been advised through Bank Task Team Leaders about the proposed workshops. The workshop is designed to assist the Government of Ethiopia in finalizing a strategy for promoting private sector participation in the Roads Sector in consultation with all stakeholders. This will be done by sharing experiences from other countries and providing expertise in different sectors.  Although the workshop would target more participants from Ethiopia, it is expected that the benefits would be equally shared through the delegations from Ghana, Uganda and Tanzania. The workshop will also benefit from the recent release of the Tool Kit for Public Private Partnership in Highways developed under PPIAF, as well as interim results from a domestic construction industry survey to be implemented with assistance of the Bank (PSD/Road sector Team) in Ethiopia in May 2002 in connection with a nationwide private firms' survey. The three-day workshop would include: (i)   Case studies from Spain, Argentina, Chad, UK, South Africa and India: presentation and discussion of experience gained in private sector participation in transport, private sector development and financing including capital markets. (ii)   Presentations given by international experts on topics related to private sector participation in roads, and issues associated with their development in different countries.. This includes: Public-Private Participation (PPP) options including performance-based maintenance contracts, contracts documentation, output based-aid, performance indicators, enabling regulatory framework, private sector capacity building, etc. (iii)   Commercialization and privatization of Direct Labor Organizations using the experience of UK. (iv)   Experience from Uganda, Tanzania, Ghana and Ethiopia : presentation and discussions of the road policy and the constraints to private sector investment in roads. (v)   Presentation given by the Chamber of Commerce and the contractors association and discussion on their perspective for the private construction industry in Ethiopia. (vi)   Overview of the Toolkit for Public Private Partnership in Highways, developed under PPIAF. column311: The proposed project supports the GoE?s vision for structural transformation of the national economy. It helps the GoE implementnew directions on agricultural development as expressed in the revised Agriculture and Rural Development Policy. The policy isaimed at (i) strengthening rural livelihoods through increasing rural incomes, ensuring food security, promoting improved nutritionand generating productive employment opportunities beyond agriculture; and (ii) transforming agriculture through accelerated growthwith sustainable use of natural resources and strong linkages with the rest of the economy.The IADP is intended to integrate thestrengthening of key agricultural value chains ensuring their competitiveness and resilience, with environmentally sustainableapproaches and enhanced rural livelihoods across diverse population groups focusing on both high performing producers andagricultural service providers as well as more vulnerable groups including women, youth and low-income households. IADP includesfour inter-related components with interventions that will lead to the above results.  The components are as follows: Component 1:Transforming Agricultural Services, Technology, and Research Systems that promote the adoption of improved agricultural practices,key to the competitiveness and resilience of supply chains through farmer-led actions. The component will focus on the entireecosystem of agricultural services, technology, and research to enable the adoption of improved and sustainable agriculturalpractices on farm and across the supply chain. It would strengthen the public and private delivery of extension services, build anew generation of extension agency by overhauling the Agricultural Technical Vocational Education and Training (ATVET) system,support plant protection and animal heath, strengthen regulatory services and support the commercialization of agriculturalresearch systems. Activities under this component will focus on (a) Promoting efficiency, outreach and efficacy in agriculturalservices through strengthening agricultural extension services, supporting agricultural training services, supporting plantprotection and animal health services and supporting public agricultural regulatory services; (b) Commercialized agriculturaltechnology generation and research system that contribute to increased productivity of crop and livestock production and improvedmanagement of natural resources. IADP will ensure a more market-oriented research system. Proposed interventions include directsupport to agricultural research activities within both public and private institutions, capacity building including inter aliapromoting and institutionalizing strong PPP, support to source technology production (breeder seed, breed, feed seed, prototype,tissue culture, micro-organisms), and promotion of mechanized agriculture technologies. IADP will also support participatoryresearch programs as well as pre-extension demonstration to enhance farmer-extension-research linkages.Component 2: ResilientRural Infrastructure Development that aimed at to address vulnerability of rural population to climate and market risks and buildresilience through supporting the development of irrigation and water harvesting infrastructure, market infrastructure development,invest in last mile physical connectivity through bridges and connecting roads for irrigated command areas, support supply chaininfrastructure, and finance institutional and governance mechanisms for management of rural infrastructure. To this end, thiscomponent will involve in (a) the development of small-scale and household irrigation infrastructures through rehabilitation of theexisting small-scale irrigation (SSI) and construction of new irrigation schemes, (b) enhance water management and infrastructuregovernance through supporting the establishment of Irrigation Water Users? Associations (IWUAs) and targeted capacity building toenable them become effective organizations, capable of managing the irrigation systems, strengthen public sector capacity forregulating the development of water resources (SSI and House-Hold Irrigation (HHI)) and support governance mechanisms for marketinfrastructure development and management; and (c) finance market and other rural infrastructure including marketcenter/infrastructure (public investment, private/joint management), cold chain infrastructure, collection centers, warehouses,silos, etc., which shall be led by the private sector through PPP arrangements. It will also support rural bridges for last mileconnectivity, and electronic marketing infrastructure.Component 3: Market and Enterprise Development aimed at to improving thecompetitiveness of strategic agricultural value chains in Ethiopia through building well-functioning agricultural markets (input,output, financial) and increases the engagement of farmers with such markets. It will support expansion of private sectorparticipation in the agri-food system, promote rural entrepreneurship (and thus create better rural non-farm job opportunities),support innovation, and help link farmers with markets. Thus, this component will provide support to ensure (a) improved marketservices, (b) enterprise development, (c) market linkages, and (d) strengthening producer groups through provision of matchinggrants, along with training and business advisory services to Common Interest Groups and commercialization of producer cooperativesand unions. This note focuses on Tigray, Amhara and SNNP region.We observed important variations in terms of firm-level productivity and investment facilitation across regions. Three factors explain these variations: (i) some business climate areas are under the mandate of the local agencies, such as land; (ii) while Investment and Business climate are ruled by a uniform set of laws and regulations decided at the Federal level, implementation is done at the regional level. The efficiency of the business climate-related areas thus depends on the capacity of the local agencies (land office, investment office and/or trade office); (iii) the constraints are more severe in some regions (road infrastructure but more broadly access to market, access to finance, etc). column5: This concept note presents a proposal for a Poverty Assessment for Ethiopia that would (i) synthesize existing work to document success in reducing poverty, (ii) undertake new analysis to understand the drivers of this success, and (iii) explore future challenges in order to inform policy that maintains and accelerate gains in poverty reduction. The focus of the assessment would be forward looking, diagnosing the recent trends in poverty reduction in order to assess how poverty reduction can be accelerated to meet ambitious poverty targets, and protected against potential shocks and challenges that the country faces. The assessment will cover the following issues: I.	A profile of the poor and ultra-poor: the Poverty Assessment will synthesize and extend work conducted over the last 18 months to answer the questions of how much poverty fell, who it fell for and the characteristics of those who are poor. Sensitivity Analysis will be conducted on trends in poverty reduction and on income growth of the bottom deciles. We will profile ultra-poor households in income deciles that have not grown during the last decade.  II.	The role of agricultural growth in poverty reduction in Ethiopia: In the last decade the GoE has pursued development policies to encourage agricultural growth, and many studies suggest that growth in this sector is often associated with poverty reduction. The assessment will undertake analysis to assess the contribution of agricultural growth to poverty reduction and the relative importance of other factors. Looking forward, can important drivers of agricultural growth be expected to continue to drive poverty reduction? Are non-farm enterprises likely to be an important driver of poverty reduction in rural areas or are they the result of improved incomes and agricultural growth? What barriers do women and the ultra-poor face in participating in rural income growth? III. Understanding and addressing urban poverty: As Ethiopia urbanizes poverty becomes a more urban phenomenon but the prevalence of urban poverty varies substantially across urban centers in Ethiopia. What is the multidimensional nature of poverty in urban areas and how this has changed over time? Urban poverty is driven by access to labor markets and this part of the report will examine urban labor markets and the characteristics of those systematically excluded from them, in order to assess the likely impact of policies to address urban poverty. IV.	Migration: For many migration reduces poverty, but those who migrate are a heterogeneous group, with some migrants, particularly girls, being vulnerable to worsening living conditions as a result of migration. The Assessment will draw on results of published and ongoing evaluations to provide insights into how to reduce the vulnerabilities associated with migration.  V.	Improved resilience, the changing nature of vulnerability in Ethiopia: This chapter will look at whether Ethiopian households have become more resilient to shocks such as droughts and food price increases? How has vulnerability in Ethiopia changed as result of recent trends in growth and what does this mean for the design of safety net programs? VI.	The impact of fiscal policy on equality: The state plays an important role in improving welfare among the very poorest and in this part of the report we will look at the incidence of government fiscal policy on households across the income distribution. The fiscal incidence study will also examine the extent to which investments in education and health benefit the poorest. The analysis will highlight policy options aimed at increasing the poverty and inequality reduction effects of fiscal policy and ensuring that these efforts are fiscally sustainable.A full task description is attached.
