column311: The proposed second phase of the Livestock and Fisheries Sector Development Project (LFSDP II) is the continuation of the on-going LFSDP. The project aims to set a functional, sustainable, and vibrant economic unit across the 5 VCs (Dairy, Poultry, Red meat, Fishery, and Apiculture) in highland and central highlands of Ethiopia in eight regions. The Development Objectives of the project (PDO) are to increase Productivity, Commercialization and Climate Resilience of Smallholder value chain actors in Livestock and Fisheries Sector in the Project Areas. The project seeks to increase productivity while building social resilience towards climate change. It also aims to address market-oriented livestock production and livestock-based agribusiness development, key national issues such as food and nutrition security, youth unemployment, poverty reduction, technology generation & adoption and economic development in livestock sector. The geographic coverage will focus on the rural and peri-urban areas of the high potential highland regions covering 184 woredas in 10 regions and 2 city administrations. The regions are Amhara, Tigray, Oromia, Benishangul, Gambella, Southwest Ethiopia, South Ethiopia, Central Ethiopia, Sidama and Harari Regions while the two city administrations are Diredawa and Addis Ababa. The total proposed financing request is US$450 million from IDA. Targeted beneficiaries include: (i) smallholder and commercial farmers; (ii) formally registered farmer cooperatives and unions. including existing cooperatives & unions formed under LFSDP-I and new members; (iii) rural youth and women (vi) Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in the project woredas that provide livestock and fishery services or inputs; (v) private sector livestock and fishery service providers, agro-processers & input dealers; and (vi) public livestock and fishery service providers. The Project will support targets to address 2 million direct and 16.8 million indirect beneficiaries. The Project will promote private-sector engagement across project regions. This engagement can address challenges pertinent to market development in more-sustainable way and support communities to achieve economic development; however, LFSDP II will not provide financial support to the private sector as well as SMEs. The support will focus on creating market linkage and capacity building for improved service delivery. Project Institutional and Implementation Arrangements: The implementing agency is the  Ministry of Agriculture (MoA). Project implementation will follow the existing Government structures. With regard to planning, implementation, and communication MoA will establish Project Coordination Units (PCUs) at Federal (FPCU), Regional (RPCU), and Woreda Levels (WPCU) to new project regions and woredas and strengthen for already existing ones. Likewise, Project Steering and Technical Committees will be established at all levels. The Agriculture Transformation Agency (ATA), the Ethiopian Cooperative Commission (ECC) and Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) will have key role in supporting the project implementation process. Likewise, Partnerships with CGIAR Center particularly ICARDA and ILRI will technically support the Project. Private actors like processors, SMEs, agro-enterprises and/or agro-industries involved in large-scale processing (and possibly located in agro-industrial parks), supermarkets, hotels, restaurants will be involved in the productive partnerships established between producers and processors/off-takers.The Project proposes three interconnected components and the fourth component focusing on Project Management, Monitoring and Evaluation and learning. Component 1 which is Transforming Livestock Values Chains for Enhanced Commercialization focus on  infrastructure development, capacity development and access to finance to value chain actors for commercialization. Primary and advanced level specialized cooperatives and unions engaged in dairy, red meat, poultry, fishery, apiculture and feed production and marketing activities will be supported. Meanwhile, livestock market infrastructure and market services will be established. Capacity building activities along with in-kind support will be provided along the targeted value chains. Component 2 will focus on Productivity and Climate Resilience. Interventions related to breed and herd improvement, animal feed, health, animal husbandry management, livestock related infrastructure development, facilities upgrading, will be supported by the component. To enhance production of genetic material and cross breeding initiative cattle dairy cross breeding farms will be strengthen and rehabilitated. Sexed embryo transfer approach will be promoted. Artificial Insemination (AI) utilization through synchronizing hormones will be supported by the regional livestock sectors. In collaboration with ICARDA and LDI, community-based breeding program (CBBP) activities will be implemented & upscaled across regions. Modernizing the service such as regional fish hatcheries, fish & aquatic life research centers, vaccine production centers and animal health clinics will be strengthened and functioning to their capacity.Component 3 will focus on Enhancing Implementation Capacity of National Programs and Services Delivery. The component will promote institutional strengthening through capacity building of the GoE,  establishment or upgrading of institutional set ups, develop livestock related policies, regulations, and plans. The institutional, organizational, and human resource capacity building support will be provided to project staff, implementing agencies and project beneficiaries. Input (including critical field equipment), extension, and advisory services will be provided to regional project coordination units and national and regional government organizations. National breeding policy and breeding strategies developed for the different livestock commodities including dairy, small ruminants, and poultry will be rolled out. Likewise, national feed resource development strategies will be developed and rolled out. Component 4 will focus on Project Coordination, Monitoring, Evaluation and Knowledge Management. Coordination of project activities will be led by Federal, Regional and Woreda level staff. The project will establish a functional M&E system with dedicated M&E specialists at Federal and Regional levels. This will ensure systematic tracking of progress, assess performance and measure impact of interventions.

column5: Since the early 1990s Ethiopia has pursued a ?developmental state? model with a strong role for the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) in many aspects of the economy. This approach, based on high levels of public investment, has been associated with strong economic growth and has delivered notable progress towards the attainment of many Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). During 2004-11 Ethiopia experienced strong and generally broad-based real economic growth averaging around 10.6 percent a year; industry and the service sector grew on average 10 percent a year, and foreign direct investment increased from US$0.5 billion in 2007 to US$1.2 billion in 2011. The growth of goods and services exports reached close to 10 percent annually during 2000-10, and Ethiopia made good progress in diversifying processed exports.The development model adopted by GoE relies heavily on high levels of largely government-led investments (like the Asian model of development), but faces low saving rates and limited availability of domestic resources (unlike the Asian model). Given the high investment requirements of the Growth and Transformation Plan (GTP), public investments, which in past years have been one of the major drivers of economic growth in Ethiopia, will not be sufficient to maintain high growth performance going forward. While private sector participation in industry and services could greatly contribute to the Government?s export-led job creation agenda, significantly leverage public sector financing and foster technology and knowledge transfer, realizing this potential will require enhancing opportunities for domestic and foreign private sector participation. There are also serious concerns that bouts of high inflation may reverse some of the positive poverty trends observed and, while inflation is currently showing a decreasing trend, keeping it down is a major challenge for macro-economic management.There has been good progress on poverty reduction and human development. Poverty in both urban and rural areas has fallen substantially from 39 percent of in 2004/05, to less than 30 percent six years later. Ethiopia is on track to achieve MDGs related to gender parity in primary education, child mortality, HIV/AIDS, and malaria. Yet, key challenges in urgent need to be addressed to ensure sustainability of the current high growth trajectory, including: ensuring macroeconomic stability; translating growth into more poverty reduction; strengthening economic competitiveness and increasing the prospects for trade; improving the quality of social services; and enhancing the capacity of the public sector.9.	The CPS highlights the need for the Bank to find ways to engage more effectively with the Government in policy dialogue on macroeconomic and private and financial sector issues. It propose to do so through by increasing the relevance of the Bank?s economic and sector work and offering the Government a menu of instruments available from across the World Bank Group. The CPS stated that, in this context, bridging the data and knowledge gap for evidence-based dialogue is key for success. The EP PKS presented in this Concept Note aims to close some of these knowledge gaps and provide the needed on-demand and timely policy advice
